chunks: "I treat every passive filter as a voltage divider made of impedances, H equals Z 2 over (Z 1 plus Z 2) , and then sanity-check with the limiting cases: a capacitor is open at DC and a short at high frequency, an inductor the opposite.
For an RC low-pass, with R in series and C to ground, I get H equals 1 over (1 plus j omega RC) .
At DC the cap is open so the gain is 1; at high frequency the cap shorts the output. The corner frequency is f c equals 1 over (2 pi RC) , where the output is down 3 decibels, 0.
707 of the input, with minus 45° of phase. Above that it rolls off at minus 20 decibels per decade.
So 1 kilohms and 159 nanofarads gives about 1 kilohertz, and at 10 kilohertz the signal is down to about 10%.
Swapping R and C gives a high-pass: H equals j omega RC over (1 plus j omega RC) , same corner, blocks DC, passes high frequencies with phase going from +90° to 0.

For a bandpass, I cascade a high-pass and a low-pass, with the corners setting the band edges, ideally with the second stage's impedance much higher or a buffer in between so they don't load each other.
Or I use a series RLC with the output across R, which peaks at 1 over square root of LC with bandwidth set by Q ."
